articles.title: Araceli raises $4.5M for drug discovery tools aimed at reducing animal testing
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Araceli Biosciences , a Portland-area biotech company, has secured $4.5 million in funding to help commercialize technology that supports using human cells instead of animal studies to test new drugs.

The Tigard, Ore., startup offers instruments and software for creating images of cells and automating analysis. Its technologies fall under the umbrella term “New Approach Methodologies,” which includes human-tissue models, computer simulations and AI-based approaches that reduce or avoid experimentation on animals such as mice, rats and monkeys.

Supporters of the methods, known as NAMs, argue that they can yield better outcomes because animals are not a perfect substitute for humans and can generate irrelevant findings. That can lead to costly, time-intensive development of drugs that fail to perform in people. Advocates also promote the alternatives as more humane.
The National Institutes of Health announced $84 million in September to build infrastructure for NAMs research at 10 sites nationwide.

“[T]he efforts signal a significant investment into human-based technologies as the future of preclinical science, aiming to make research faster, more predictive, and more directly relevant to human health,” the NIH said in a release .

Araceli has raised a total of $18.76 million from investors, and the new round was led by William Cortelyou and included Fluke Venture Partners, according to PitchBook. The company disclosed Thursday that businessman and animal welfare advocate Jeff Swickard was also an investor.
Swickard owns 54 auto dealerships across Western states and is a commercial real estate investor with $250 million invested in Portland properties.
Shawn MacDonald, chief financial officer for Araceli, said Swickard’s “support reflects a belief that we share, which is that better science and more humane science go hand-in-hand.”
Araceli launched in 2023 as a spinoff from Phoseon Technology, which makes UV LED units for industrial curing and life sciences applications.

The company says it has a strong presence in the Bay Area, Boston, London and Berlin, and that half of the world’s top 20 pharmaceutical companies use its technology. It has 38 employees, according to PitchBook.

articles.title: Uncommon Thinkers: Alexis Harroun aims for space with a new engine — and stays grounded
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners .

A few weeks after learning that her tiny startup had won a NASA prize to fly its engine in space, Alexis Harroun was camping in Yellowstone, sitting around a fire and looking up at the stars. Satellites kept drifting past overhead — and the news finally sank in.
“I’m like, oh, we’re going to be sending something up and we’re going to be able to see it,” she said. “That was very humbling in a lot of ways and very exciting.”

Harroun is co-founder and CEO of Juno Propulsion , a Tukwila, Wash.-based startup building a new kind of rocket engine. Instead of burning fuel in a steady flame, Juno’s engines use detonation, a supersonic combustion wave that releases more energy from the same amount of propellant.
“It’s essentially like a higher MPG rocket engine,” Harroun said.

The technology has been studied for decades but has never flown in orbit. Juno aims to change that next year, when its engine is set to fly aboard a Momentus satellite in a mission called Project Iris .
That’s a big goal for a company that, when the July 2025 NASA call came , was just Harroun, co-founder and CTO Ari Martinez and a summer intern working out of a one-room office.

If Iris succeeds, Juno’s engines could let satellites run on non-toxic fuel and maneuver far more freely in orbit, something both commercial and defense customers increasingly want. For Harroun, who earned her Ph.D. studying these engines, it would be the payoff of years of work.

Harroun sees the technology as a long-overdue leap. The basic physics behind today’s rocket engines dates to the 1930s and has been refined about as far as it can go, she said, calling it a constraint that’s “been a glass ceiling for too long, in my opinion.”

Harroun grew up south of Seattle in Federal Way. She didn’t come from an aerospace family or spend her childhood dreaming about space. Her dad was a physician and her mom a flight attendant and flight instructor.

What she did pick up at home was an entrepreneurial streak. Her dad ran his own practice for about 20 years, and her mom is now a real estate agent. Harroun said watching them make “something out of completely nothing” has shaped her own path, especially in building Juno.

She calls herself a “late bloomer” who fell for engineering as she was finishing high school and heading to the University of Washington. Sci-fi became an inspiration along the way, and it’s now one of her favorite genres.

She spent all four years at UW working with professor Carl Knowlen , who leads the Aeronautics & Astronautics Department’s Detonation Engines Lab, and she joined the student rocketry team, eventually leading its propulsion group.

Knowlen “sees the potential in everyone,” Harroun said, and the two built a strong relationship that’s still going. Juno’s $1.2 million National Science Foundation grant , awarded this summer, is a partnership with his research group.

“What’s exciting is seeing this come full circle,” Knowlen said in a 2025 UW story . “Alexis’s passion for this technology grew out of our lab work together, and now we’re collaborating to turn that early research into something that will fly in space.”
During college, Harroun interned at NASA, Boeing and Blue Origin. That first stint at Blue Origin, in 2016, set her next move.
“I realized that everyone who had the job that I wanted had gone to Purdue,” she said.

She spent the next six years at Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind., earning a master’s degree and a Ph.D. Her doctoral research was on the technology Juno is now building. She also met Martinez there. The two shared an office for years.
Harroun never planned to stay in academia.
“That just didn’t feel like my calling,” she said. “I wanted to use that very unique experience to get the technical chops to do the type of engineering that I wanted to do.”
Her doctoral advisor, Purdue professor Stephen Heister , still advises her and the company.

“He was one of the people who really pushed me to think about starting this company,” Harroun said. “I think he saw the potential that I had as a founder, both from a technical and a leadership perspective.”

Heister recalled their first technical discussion, when Harroun arrived as a new master’s student. He went deep on nozzle flows, her thesis topic, and the complications of building a nozzle for a detonation engine.

“At the end of my diatribe, she sat quietly and said, ‘You’ve given me a lot to think about,’” Heister said. “I can’t think of any other 22-year-old student with such a response but I knew she was indeed a special talent.”
He described Harroun as having “the unique ability to think deeply and at length,” and said it’s “terribly gratifying” to watch her commercialize the technology she worked on as a grad student.

After finishing her Ph.D. in 2023, Harroun came back to the Seattle region and started Juno. She knew the territory: her UW lab work and the rocketry team had put her in touch with local industry, and Juno now works with some of the same companies she did as a student.

Interning at Blue Origin was the first time she could say “there’s literally a rocket company in our backyard,” Harroun said. Its presence helped build a regional talent pool, which she described as “a contingent of rocket scientists that just live here.”
Starting a company comes with many unknowns, and coming home crossed one off the list.
“I knew how to go start doing stuff immediately,” she said. “So it made that calculus really easy.”
Harroun’s ambitions reach well beyond one demo flight.
“Our mission is to be the rocket engine provider for the U.S.,” she said. “Think of a Rocketdyne.”

That company built engines for the Saturn V and the space shuttle, and it’s now part of L3Harris . Juno wants to play a similar role with a new technology. It’s starting with in-space propulsion for satellites and plans to expand into engines for upper stages, orbital transfer vehicles and, eventually, the boosters that lift rockets off the pad.

The first step is Project Iris. NASA paid Juno about $500,000 through its TechLeap program to build the payload, and it’s also covering the Momentus spacecraft and the flight. There’s no paying customer yet, but the mission is designed to mimic the maneuvers a real satellite would make.
Japan’s space agency has flown rotating detonation engines on suborbital research rockets, but going to orbit is “a whole ‘nother game,” Harroun said. “Going to space is hard. I can attest to that.”

Building a company has taught Harroun things her Ph.D. didn’t. Handling toxic propellants is so complicated, she learned, that operators can spend more fueling a satellite than on “the propulsion system itself, which is kind of crazy.”
The bigger draw is mobility. For decades, satellites have mostly stayed in the orbit a rocket left them in, she said, and “that’s not really acceptable anymore in today’s world.”
To get there, Juno has raised a $1.4 million pre-seed round led by SOSV, on top of its NASA and NSF awards.
As for going to space herself, Harroun admits it would be hard to say no if she got the opportunity.
But the avid hiker and backpacker is partial to terra firma. Her best-case future is one where Earth is the place humanity gets to enjoy and space is what makes that possible.
“I don’t know that I would be the traveler,” Harroun said, “but I’d definitely like to be the enabler.”

articles.title: ‘A huge pain in the ass’: Microsoft 365 starts to recover after a day of global email turmoil
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: If emails sent by Outlook users on Thursday are just now landing in your inbox, no, you haven’t gone back to the days of the Pony Express. Microsoft is still digging out from a nearly daylong outage that cut off email for businesses, schools and governments around the world.
As of early Friday, the company reported that email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels,” though some users could still have trouble getting in or see delayed messages.

In a post on X Friday morning, Microsoft said it was “deeply sorry” for the disruption to customers and partners. The company said the outage was a technical issue, not related to a cyberattack or AI agents.

The problem was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a more recent network change, the company said, adding that it has addressed the underlying issue and is still restoring service to remaining customers and regions.

In an update on its status page at 5 a.m. Pacific, Microsoft said it was seeing “broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe,” along with early signs of recovery in Asia Pacific.

The problems started Thursday morning with Exchange Online, the Microsoft service that runs Outlook email for businesses, and spread to other Microsoft 365 services that depend on it, including Teams calendars, Copilot and SharePoint.

Microsoft said servers were failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, which overloaded the ones that were left. The company paused all deployments while it worked on a fix, and some of its repairs Thursday evening were “not taking as expected.”
Microsoft has promised a full post-incident report once its review is complete.
Earlier, The Verge’s Tom Warren reported on X that his sources linked the outage to configuration changes in Azure Virtual Network, Microsoft’s cloud networking service.

Australia’s Home Affairs Minister, Tony Burke, told reporters in Sydney that Microsoft believes it is dealing with something similar in some ways to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, “where there is an update that has gone awry,” the Associated Press reported .

“We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us,” said Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, in a statement provided to GeekWire. He said Microsoft’s teams are reviewing what happened and how to prevent similar problems.

The outage reached well beyond email. Government offices in Japan, Singapore and the Philippines reported disruptions, according to the AP. Workhorse Group delayed its quarterly earnings call, and OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools.

Credit rating agency Morningstar DBRS estimated insured losses of $300 million to $500 million, well below estimates for CrowdStrike, which ranged from $400 million to $1.5 billion. Some cyber insurance policies cover only malicious attacks, the firm noted, though it said the toll could grow if the outage drags on for several days.

The disruption hit close to Microsoft’s home. Ansel Herz, a spokesperson for the Seattle mayor’s office, told the Seattle Times that the outage didn’t bring city government to a halt but knocked out the systems that move documents and messages around City Hall.
The newspaper quoted Herz calling the outage “a huge pain.” In a post on X , he chided the paper for not using his whole quote, which we presume was “a huge pain in the ass.”
We’ve followed up with him to confirm this important detail. Here’s hoping he gets the email.

Update, 10 a.m.: Herz did receive GeekWire’s message and responded, confirming the quote and saying that, to his knowledge, nothing public-facing was affected at the city. Email appears to be back and working properly as of Friday morning, he said.

articles.title: Five More Washington Cities Selected for State Growth Plan Reviews in 2027
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Washington's Commerce Department has released a list of five cities and towns that will see their housing growth plans subjected to additional state scrutiny next year, the second set of reviews planned under the 2025 Housing Accountability Act . Burlington, Friday Harbor, Mount Vernon, Oak Harbor, and Washougal will go under the microscope, with city leaders given deadlines to make any updates to their local Comprehensive Plans with the goal of ensuring that development regulations intended to pave the way for more diverse housing types across a range of income levels are in place.

The 2027 cities are mostly clustered around the north end of Puget Sound, in counties that had a state-mandated December 31, 2025 deadline to overhaul their local Comprehensive Plans. All five cities faced that deadline and didn't meet it, either leaving Commerce out of the loop when it comes to updating their plan or submitting a draft plan that the state found to fall short in some way.

The Housing Accountability Act represents something of a sea change in local housing growth planning that cities are still getting used to. Prior to its implementation, the only way to challenge a Comprehensive Plan that looked to be out-of-compliance with state law was to file a challenge at the state's Growth Management Hearings Board, a case-by-case appeal process that usually fell on private groups like neighborhood organizations or the statewide land use advocacy non-profit Futurewise to pursue.

Though the Commerce Department is often tasked with providing recommendations on local development standards and zoning changes, there wasn't a mechanism available to hold cities and towns that went too far their own way accountable. With the Housing Accountability Act, cities and towns are given a compliance deadline to make essential changes and if those aren't enacted, the so-called Builder's Remedy goes into effect – with local permit departments unable to deny building permits for residential projects that meet certain affordability requirements, regardless of the underlying zoning. Theoretically, that could mean skyscrapers in areas of the city that aren't used to dense housing.

Commerce is still in the middle of its 2026 "selected review" process, with zoning changes already adopted in three of the eight jurisdictions that made the list this year. So far, only Carnation has gotten to the stage of approving a final plan that is still being reviewed by Commerce, with Bainbridge Island and the 300-resident town of Beaux Arts Village both adopting interim regulations that provide additional time to adopt permanent changes down the road.

Next week, the City of DuPont, tucked into South Pierce County near Joint Base Lewis-McChord, is poised to be the first city to actually trigger the Builder's Remedy. Despite a timeline that doesn't call for adoption of potential changes to the city's Comprehensive Plan until early next year, DuPont has not requested an extension from Commerce that would prevent the Builder's Remedy from taking effect.

Though many of the jurisdictions that have been subjected to review so far have been relatively small, the impact is adding up. By the end of the second year, Commerce is on track to have reviewed cities and towns accounting for approximately 144,000 residents, more people than live in Washington's sixth largest city of Kent.

In turning its attention to Friday Harbor, Commerce will be jumping into the fray when it comes to one of the state's thorniest housing crises. As a tourist-oriented city with a high rate of seasonal housing, housing in Friday Harbor is regularly out-of-reach of the workers that the local economy relies on. Housing prices within San Juan County rose more than 100% between 2016 and 2022, far faster than median wages could ever compete with.

Despite increased demand for units in Friday Harbor, projects proposed in the city often turn highly contentious. Last year, a 49-unit development near Friday Harbor elementary school drew significant opposition, despite the inclusion of eight units of workforce housing in the project. The concerns raised included increased traffic, traffic safety impacts, and a lack of overall infrastructure, but the common denominator was the idea that Friday Harbor can't handle more population density.

Amanda Lynn, Executive Director of the San Juan Community Home Trust, offered an overall view of housing growth on San Juan Island, in an interview with the The Journal of the San Juans about that specific project.

“Every time you add a housing unit on this island, that requires infrastructure, that requires community resources like fire, police, school, anything you can think of,” Lynn said. “Every housing unit requires these things. So there’s always a balance beyond even just thinking about the ecosystem balance of the island itself.”
That balancing act, while clearly necessary in some regard on a ferry-dependent island, often means that lower-income residents trying to find homes in San Juan Island get the short end of the stick.

A state review under the Housing Accountability Act won't be able to fully solve Friday Harbor's housing crisis, of course. But it will likely ensure that barriers that stand in the way of housing production that aren't aligned with state law don't stay in place, adding clear repercussions if they do.

As these reviews continue to ramp up, pushback from local elected officials is another thing to watch for. As Beaux Arts Village councilmembers took their vote on interim development regulations last month, they also vowed to push for legislative changes that would modify the Housing Accountability Act to be less impactful on them. So far, what exactly it would look like to water down the legislation hasn't become clear, but as larger cities start to get subjected to that review, the political pressure could ramp up.

For now, however, the Housing Accountability Act does appear to be having its intended impact, slowly bringing along jurisdictions that otherwise would be lagging when it comes to legalizing housing, one by one.

articles.title: Nailed it: Muse Crush expanding to Capitol Hill with ‘almost overwhelming’ selection of press-on nails
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: “The first and only handmade press-on nail store in Seattle” is expanding to Capitol Hill.
Muse Crush is bringing its crafted and unique press-on nail sets and collectibles to E Pike. The shop’s signature pink paint job is already complete.

Seattle entrepreneur Jinger Zhao founded the business online in 2022 before opening a storefront on NE 43rd in the U-District. An “amazing, gorgeous, almost overwhelming selection,” one review from a shopper reads.

The press-on nail boutique and “Japanese-inspired kawaii cute, and creative gift shop” will replace Capitol Hill’s only self-serve kombucha taproom. Portland-born SOMA Kombucha shuttered its taps following a late 2025 run-in with a SUV that smashed into the storefront.

Muse Crush Capitol Hill will soon neighbor Sal’s Barbershop and HoneyHole just down the block from Doghouse Leathers and Babeland at the corner of E Pike and Boylston. Just look for Mina, the giant blue lounging cat in the mural around the corner from the newly-painted-pink storefront.

Unlike mass-produced drugstore strips, Muse Crush’s nail sets are handmade with hand-painted artwork including creations from local artists, plus sculpted finishes, and 3D charms, and are sold in sizes from extra-small to large across short and long lengths. Priced around $28 to $30, each set includes adhesive tabs, a nail file, and a wooden cuticle stick.
Beyond nails, the shop stocks blind-box figurines, plush keychains, jewelry, stickers, and goods from local creators.
Muse Crush will open soon at 701 E Pike. Learn more at musecrush.co .

articles.title: Wilson’s veto stands as Seattle City Council tussles over flipped vote
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Mayor Katie Wilson’s veto of Seattle City Council legislation to create a parking permit system for people living homeless in RVs will stand.
The council voted 5–4 on Thursday to sustain the veto falling a vote short of the majority needed to enact street parking limits and the permitting system for RVs.
District 3 Councilmember and Council President Joy Hollingsworth voted to override the veto, joining Councilmembers Debora Juarez, Bob Kettle, Maritza Rivera, and bill sponsor Dan Strauss .

Ahead of the vote, residents, service providers, and business representatives weighed in during a packed hybrid public comment session limited to one-minute addresses per speaker. The majority urged the council to uphold the veto, contending that Seattle lacks sufficient safe parking lots and shelter beds. Outreach workers and unhoused residents warned that tying permits to a rigid, one-time census would lead to towed and impounded homes.

Speaking to conditions in District 3, one commenter who works with unhoused individuals in Cal Anderson Park argued against banning RVs as a form of “collective punishment” when residents already face severe instability.
Business leaders from Ballard and North Seattle urged an override to curb illegal drug markets and neighborhood blight.

Wilson has matched her veto with an executive order focused on immediate service deployment rather than administrative permitting. The order directs city departments to immediately release 2026 outreach funding, fast-track the opening and occupancy of two RV safe lots designed to accommodate 182 residents, and establish a cross-departmental and community working group to troubleshoot right-of-way conditions and address neighborhood impacts using existing laws.

During debate Thursday, Hollingsworth rejected claims that the legislation passed by the council and vetoed by Wilson was punitive, arguing that preserving the status quo fails both vehicle residents and frustrated neighbors. Pointing to the city’s $228 million homelessness budget and calling the King County Regional Homeless Authority’s execution a “complete disaster,” she demanded accountability and tangible results.
“It might make us feel good about allocating millions of dollars, but without outcomes, now that is cruel and inhumane,” Hollingsworth said.

With progressive-leaning Councilmembers Alexis Mercedes Rinck, Eddie Lin, and Dionne Foster voting no, West Seattle’s Rob Saka represented a key swing vote, joining the “no” side against overturning the veto after previously voting for the original bill.

Saka praised sponsor Strauss for a “herculean effort” on the legislative package while explaining his own decision to flip his vote and sustain the mayor’s veto. Saka framed his shift as exercising the “humility and grace to change your mind” to give the mayor’s executive order a fair shot — emphasizing human dignity, a “carrot and stick” balance of compassion and accountability, and geographic equity for his heavily impacted District 1.

Tensions flared during closing remarks when Strauss argued that the mayor’s 60-day task force could easily run concurrently with his bill’s built-in review period, characterizing the argument that sustaining the veto represented a “new path” as “duplicitous” and a vote for the status quo.

Following a point of order raised by Lin over council rules against impugning colleagues’ motives, a visibly frustrated Saka scolded Strauss for “Seattle passive aggressive, subtle slights,” challenging him to take any grievances up directly in their adjacent offices rather than questioning his character or integrity. Strauss maintained that he was merely pointing out a factual overlap in policy timelines rather than attacking Saka’s motives.

The RV debate comes as the council is winding up final changes to the mayor’s 2027-2028 budget plan including tapping $31 million in JumpStart payroll tax reserves and cutting $22 million in pension transfers to reverse cuts proposed by Wilson to address a looming budget deficit.

It also arrives as the Wilson administration is shifting its strategies around homelessness including expanded timelines for reaching shelter goals and changes in how encampment removals are prioritized as parks like Cal Anderson generate more than 1,000 citizen complaints about illegal encampments per year.
With the veto holding, attention now shifts to Wilson’s executive order to expand outreach and safe parking alternatives.

articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: To plan the next generation of north-south travel in western Washington, the Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) is working on the I-5 Master Plan and the Cascadia High Speed Rail project. As a result, WSDOT is leading the effort while working with agencies in Oregon and British Columbia.

articles.title: Katie Wilson’s RV Ban Veto Survives!
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: On Thursday, the Seattle City Council officially declined to override Mayor Katie Wilson’s veto , killing the effective RV ban it passed last month. Bill sponsor Dan Strauss, who was very upset about the whole thing, garnered only five votes for the override, failing to meet the two-thirds threshold he needed to override a mayoral veto.

Everyone saw this coming after Councilmember Rob Saka’s last-minute change of position on the ordinance last week. It puts an end to a bruising political fight between Wilson and Strauss, who is also the council’s budget chair.

The vote ensures hundreds of homeless Seattleites who live in RVs and other large vehicles won’t have to enroll in a specialized permitting system to retain the right to park for 72 hours on city streets. Advocates said the proposed system—which would have only allowed people surveyed in a one-time census to obtain a permit— wouldn’t work for most RV residents who are transient and may lack other forms of paperwork.

Wilson issued the veto against the bill— her first as mayor— because the permitting system would be difficult to enforce, legally risky, expensive (costing about $3.5 million over the next five years), and could drive more people into unsheltered homelessness. The city charter required the council to vote on Wilson’s veto within 30 days.

Despite losing the veto vote, Strauss succeeded in passing most of his legislative agenda on RV resident reforms, including four ordinances and one non-binding resolution. These changes include adding more funding for vehicle resident outreach, authorizing city-owned vehicle storage lots, and updating the city’s definition of “junk vehicles” to streamline parking enforcement. Strauss’s proposal for a working group was also incorporated in Wilson’s executive order signed last week. An interim report is due in early January, with final recommendations expected by the end of March.

Wilson’s veto came after fierce opposition from homeless service providers, vehicle residents, and other progressive advocates. Alison Eisinger, executive director of the Seattle/King County Coalition on Homelessness, says that as of yesterday, constituents had sent more than 4,700 emails to council members and the mayor. About 30 people testified at yesterday’s special meeting, with most speaking against the RV ban.

Prior to the vote, council members spent about an hour relitigating their perspectives on the legislation. Strauss stubbornly defended his bill, saying “doing nothing is not an option.” He also compared advocates’ concerns about the “harmful” and “draconian” nature of the permitting system to the type of complaints middle-class neighbors tend to lodge against new shelter and affordable housing.

“These are the same concerns of complexity, of expense, of potential harmful impacts that I have literally heard about setting up tiny house villages [and] providing medically assisted treatment at shelters,” Strauss said.

Other moderates on the council reiterated their positions. Councilmember Bob Kettle said the impacts on neighborhoods by RV residents needed to be considered; Councilmembers Maritza Rivera and Debora Juarez said drug dealing, sex trafficking, and other crimes were being committed in RVs. Juarez, an interim appointee who will be replaced by newly elected progressive Nilu Jenks in two weeks, also had choice words for Wilson’s leadership, saying the public would see her veto as “dishonesty, inconsistency, [and] lack of leadership.”

The three progressives on the council, while (thankfully) less verbose, also stuck to their same talking points before the vote. Councilmember Dionne Foster said the one-time nature of the permitting system was a deal breaker, as it would exclude future families who may become homeless and have to live in their vehicles. Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck thanked advocates for their testimony, while Councilmember Eddie Lin called for unity despite policy disagreements.
Saka, whose pivotal flip-flop changed the outcome of the vote, said leadership is in part about “having the humility and grace to change your mind if new information becomes available.”

His comments seemed to anger Strauss, who responded that calling the mayor’s veto “‘a new path’ is duplicitous.” In a point of order, Saka accused Strauss of impugning his motives, motivation, and character, which is against the council’s decorum rules. What’s a council meeting without a little drama, right?
Strauss’s comments angered activists, too. Chanel Horner, a human rights advocate and former vehicle resident who currently lives in a tiny home, saw it as a false equivalence.
“He tried to compare us to Republicans, and that was unfounded,” Horner said. “Republicans are like ‘not in my backyard.’ We’re basically the opposite.”

Eisinger also took issue with the stigmatizing framing of RV residents as a public safety issue; instead of going through the council’s human services committee, Strauss’s bill was passed by the public safety committee. She says serious crime should be investigated and dealt with regardless of if the perpetrator lives in a house or a vehicle.

Now that Strauss’s bill is dead, where will the money for establishing the permitting program go? Strauss sponsored a budget provision to prevent Wilson from spending the roughly $800,000 a year on other purposes. He wants the RV working group to release its recommendations before unlocking those funds, which will require another vote by the city council.

Here’s an idea: Services and shelter for homeless vehicle residents are woefully underfunded. After a year and a half without any safe lots in the city, the Low Income Housing Institute is set to open Glassyard Commons in West Seattle later this month, which will have 72 spots available.

The city is setting aside funding for a second safe lot to open next year, which Horner argued should go to a different service provider so that homeless people have multiple options to choose from. But even that won’t be enough, she says, and ultimately there just isn’t enough housing available for everyone living on the streets.
“If we just had more housing, we’d have somewhere to move people to,” Horner said. “We wouldn’t have to be in an RV in the first place.”

articles.title: Seattle’s Leaders are Notably Absent from Nationwide Boycott of Starbucks Over Labor Abuses
articles.author: Hunter Pauli
paras: After years of organizing and prolonged contract negotiations over better working conditions, Starbucks Workers United (SBWU) union members announced a nationwide boycott campaign in late August calling on allies to force the fast food company to the negotiating table.

Starbucks workers rallied at 40 college campuses nationwide yesterday, including the University of Washington, calling on administrators to put ties with the coffee chain over its labor abuses. Seattle City Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck spoke at the UW rally in support of the boycott and urged the university to kick Starbucks off campus.

Politicians across the country are joining the boycott, including seven sitting congressmen and six new ones, as well as two US senators (none of these are local) and city councils across the country. Several state-level Democratic parties, including Washington’s, are part of the boycott, according to a recent count.
But here in Seattle, where the company was founded and remains based, the political class isn’t so quick to join.
Among local politicians, King County Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda and Washington House Rep. Shaun Scott have publicly joined the boycott, though it’s not exactly a big club.
But the most notable absent voice is Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson.

Among Wilson’s first acts after being elected mayor was to announce at an SBWU strike rally that she was boycotting Starbucks and that others should too. Notably there was no active nationwide boycott campaign called by SBWU when Wilson said “I am not buying Starbucks, and you should not either,” last November.

Over the next six months, Wilson was smeared by conservative media for advocating a boycott of a local corporation over its poor labor record. This included a column in the Wall Street Journal ‘s notoriously right-wing editorial pages written by former Starbucks owner Howard Schultz.

“Seattle’s mayor, Katie Wilson, has chosen to cast business as a foil rather than a partner. Her socialist rhetoric vilifies employers, even while she continues to rely on them for revenue,” Schultz wrote.

The attacks on Wilson are consistent with an ongoing campaign by business leaders opposing progressive taxation of Seattle’s corporate titans, who have spun a narrative of growing capital flight to the libertarian climates of the former Confederacy.

Wilson denounced her own prior support for a Starbucks boycott to the New York Times in May of this year, calling her words “not productive in the sense that they caused more harm than good,” and saying she wants “a multidimensional relationship” with local corporations.

“Multidimensional” is an accurate self-assessment, as the Mayor’s Office has, in recent months, assumed a quantum superposition of pledging to support unionization efforts at Starbucks while simultaneously walking back Wilson’s prior support for a boycott, a tactic Starbucks workers are now using to pressure the company.

In a FOX 13 interview broadcast June 3, Wilson told the interviewer “I guess I broke my boycott” by ordering a blueberry muffin latte during a visit to Starbucks’ Pike Place Market location when she went to the store “to talk to the workers there who are organizing a union.”
Since ending her spontaneous boycott this summer, SBWU announced their official nationwide boycott campaign, and the mayor’s nebulous position on the matter has only become more unclear.

At a recent press conference, Wilson refused to answer a direct question from The Stranger as to whether she was or was not boycotting Starbucks in light of the union’s new boycott campaign and her prior support.

“I absolutely support Starbucks workers’ right to organize and to join a union, and I want to see the union and the company bargaining in good faith and getting to a fair contract,” she said, declining to answer the question again when pressed.
Asked when she last went to Starbucks, Wilson said she did not remember.

Despite the hedging, giving no response when asked if she’s boycotting Starbucks effectively means the mayor is sticking with her prior decision to end her boycott, even if saying so publicly has now been made politically unfeasible by SBWU’s formal boycott campaign.

SBWU isn’t rushing to throw Wilson under the bus however, or, at least, leadership isn’t. Asked for comment on the mayor’s recent cryptic statements, SBWU told The Stranger “Mayor Katie Wilson has long stood shoulder-to-shoulder with union baristas, including on the picket line, and we’re proud to have her support in our fight for a fair contract.”

The statement continued: “Our union movement has taken the nation by storm, and the Starbucks boycott continues to grow in strength as elected officials, state parties, unions and consumers nationwide put their weight behind us and show their commitment to working people everywhere. Together, we will continue to fight for a fair contract that addresses systemic challenges like understaffing, low pay, unpredictable hours and more.”

While she is a self-proclaimed socialist, Wilson’s summertime reneging on her Starbucks boycott exemplifies that she is not a product of the labor movement, the traditional incubator of socialist politics. On October 1, the Washington State Labor Council announced the powerful state union federation was joining the boycott until baristas win a fair contract. Other major labor groups joining the boycott include the AFL-CIO and SEIU.

Until the union’s demands are met, SBWU is calling on boycotters to “run a Starbucks-free organization,” not contract with the company, encourage others to join, and “show up and show out to help union baristas win a fair contract.”

articles.title: Slog AM: Microsoft Outage Persists, Sound Transit Tries to Stop Killing Fish, A Schumer Challenger Appears
articles.author: Nathalie Graham
paras: Horse thief in Portland: A 29-year-old Idaho woman was visiting Portland for a model horse show. She brought her whole collection of 100 custom, hand-painted model horses worth $10,000 and won best-in-show. The next day, someone smashed her car window and stole her entire collection , hawking “piles of her horses” on the street for $5. Police arrested a suspect. Please, if you obtained a beautiful model horse in the Pearl District, return it to its rightful owner.

Fuck this grifter: Right-wing influencer Nick Shirley has retracted his claim that he witnessed food stamp fraud at Seattle grocery store Lam’s Seafood Asian Market. The video retraction comes a month and millions of views after Shirley made the claim. It also came after Lam’s hired a lawyer and threatened to sue Shirley.

A grim Outlook: Microsoft is entering day two of a global outage that’s hobbling Outlook, Teams, and AI assistant Copilot. As of Friday morning, the company said it was making “headway” on restoring services. This little technological world we’ve built is so fragile. Enjoy your work holiday, Outlook users.
Due to the Microsoft outage, Japanese stock markets are switching to fax machines .

ICYMI: Did you know that when its staff tried to unionize, immigration nonprofit Washington Immigration Solidarity Network hired a law firm known for busting unions, and paid them thousands of dollars despite a year of financial hardship? Cedar Attanasio and Hunter Pauli have the story here .

Fish fry: Sound Transit is trying to mitigate the fish electrocution happening underneath the crosslake connection. The agency believes underwater wires known as anodes are zapping and killing fish that swim by them. Sound Transit is installing 13 mesh tube cages to encase those wires and prevent fish deaths. If these work, they’ll install mesh tubes on all 113 pontoon anode strings, reports KUOW .

AG won’t defend trans sports ban: Attorney General Nick Brown will not defend Initiative 638, the trans sports ban, against the lawsuit brought by the ACLU of Washington, Legal Voice, and Pacifica Law Group. Brown said he has conflicts of interest since his office has argued against trans sports bans in the past and Brown’s former employer, Pacifica Law Group, is part of the suit.
The weather: Today it will be wet. The weekend will be wet. Seattle!

Lay a flower on his Nvidia grave : Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—the only CEO the chipmaker has ever had—has resigned after reports that he was honeypotted by a Chinese spy and subsequent reports about affairs he had with a subordinate and a member of the board. Huang has been summoned to testify before Congress about “serious” national security concerns .

Buck Chuck: That’s Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s plan. The Maryland senator has announced he’ll challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer for majority leader. He has the support of progressives in the Senate like Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Sen. Bernie Sanders. Schumer remains confident he has the votes to win.
Brooklyn building collapse death toll rises: Eight people are dead after an apartment building collapsed in Brooklyn’s Flatbush neighborhood on Wednesday.

Data centers on public lands: Interior Secretary Doug Burgmun wants to build data centers on public lands controlled by the federal government. Burgmun is heavily invested in the AI industry and seems singularly focused on building up data centers, in spite of public opinion souring on them.

Should we drain Lake Powell? The lake on the Utah-Arizona border formed after the 1960s construction of the Glen Powell dam flooded Glen Canyon. It’s now a pivotal source for hydroelectric power and a key reservoir for Lower Basin states. But drought has made Lake Powell less reliable. This summer, it reached a record low—almost so low that water wouldn’t be able to flow through the Glen Powell Dam to create hydroelectric power. That drought will likely worsen. Low water levels also reduce levels in Lake Mead, another key reservoir, to help prop up Powell. Groups are calling for Lake Powell to be drained . They say it will restore the Colorado River, help Lake Mead, and uncover Glen Canyon.
A self-plug for your Friday: If you are need of Friday plans, why not come watch an improv show at the Fremont Abbey? I’ll be in this one .

articles.title: Why the Microsoft 365 outage is different and why it takes so long to restore email services
articles.author:
<name>Doug Jacobson, University Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Iowa State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/doug-jacobson-809162"/>
paras: The Microsoft services outage that began on Nov. 12, 2026, is not like other internet outages. The failure affected the Microsoft 365 suite of productivity services, including the video conferencing and collaboration platform Teams, AI assistant Copilot and, significantly, the Outlook email service.

Microsoft reported on Nov. 13 that the company is “continuing to see improvements in service availability” but that “some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery.”

Despite decades of predictions about its decline , email remains a central pillar of how organizations function. Password resets, invoices, legal notices and cybersecurity incident response coordination all depend on it. The Microsoft 365 outage affected businesses, governments and schools around the world.

When most people think about cloud outages , they picture a broken website or a stalled app. When the service going down includes email, however, the mechanics of the failure and how to recover from it are different from those of almost every other cloud service.
Unlike modern web apps or authentication gatekeepers, email wasn’t designed to fail fast, meaning to immediately halt when a problem arises.

When a typical cloud service breaks , it acts like a closed door. If an authentication provider or a cloud application goes down, users are immediately locked out and see an error message. Access stops. When people cannot get into the system, they are not actively generating new work or adding heavy processing loads to the broken servers. Once engineers fix the underlying bug and unlock the door, traffic can resume and the service often recovers fairly quickly.
Email does not have a closed door. It is built on an older, decentralized “store-and-forward” architecture designed to never lose a message, even when the destination is unreachable.

Because email is a network of thousands of independent systems, an outage at one major provider does not stop users on other platforms from hitting “send.” During major email disruptions like the one that hit Microsoft, millions of outside users on Gmail, corporate servers or other platforms could still compose and send emails to affected accounts without seeing an immediate error message.

From the sender’s perspective, everything works normally. Their email provider accepts the message, attempts to hand it off to the downed provider, realizes the destination isn’t answering, and quietly holds onto the message in an outbound queue to try again later.

One way to think about email traffic in outages is to imagine a multilane interstate highway where an accident blocks two lanes of traffic. Drivers miles away don’t stop leaving their driveways just because there is a wreck up ahead; they keep entering the highway system. Soon, traffic backs up so severely that metered on-ramps have to stop letting new cars merge onto the interstate. Before long, that gridlock spills backward onto local feeder roads and city streets, choking traffic miles away from the actual crash site.

In this analogy, a downed email provider is the crash. Every other email server around the world is an on-ramp or a feeder road. While the outage lasts, millions of messages continue to pile up in queues across the internet, with unaffected servers repeatedly resending email to see whether traffic is moving yet.

When engineers finally fix the root cause of an email outage, it is the equivalent of tow trucks clearing the wreckage from the highway. The road is technically open again, but traffic does not instantly return to normal speed.

First, the massive backlog of vehicles already stuck on the main highway has to start moving. Only after that congestion clears can the on-ramps start letting queued-up cars merge back in, which in turn slowly relieves the gridlock on the surrounding local roads.

Similarly, when a major email provider comes back online, it is immediately hit with a tidal wave of pent-up messages and retry attempts from every other mail server on the internet. Processing those queues without overwhelming the newly restored servers takes time – typically hours to days.

Because organizations have largely outsourced their email to a small number of global providers, an outage doesn’t just disrupt one company; it can stall entire sectors at once, cutting off the communication tool teams rely on to coordinate their emergency response.

And for everyday users, this unique architecture explains why email failures feel so drawn out: Even hours after a provider officially announces a problem is fixed, messages can still arrive out of order or trickle in slowly as the digital traffic jam finally clears.

articles.title: Oceans and forests have absorbed roughly half our carbon emissions for decades, slowing climate change – but can they keep it up?
articles.author:
<name>Andrew C. Manning, Visiting Professor of Carbon Cycle Science, Rochester Institute of Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/andrew-c-manning-2682459"/>
paras: Over the past two centuries, humans have pumped billions of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere by burning fossil fuels , raising global temperatures in the process.
Luckily for humanity, Earth has done what it could to soften the impact.
The world’s oceans have absorbed 35% of carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels since 1990, our new research shows, and the forests and other plants of the world have absorbed another 13%.

The importance of these two enormous natural carbon sinks cannot be overstated as global temperatures rise, fueling heat waves, fires, storms, floods and droughts around the world. Yet there is much that scientists do not understand about these carbon sinks – most importantly, how exactly they’ll behave in the future.

If the oceans and forests keep absorbing the same amount of carbon dioxide, scientists will have a sense of what to expect in the future and what can be done to slow climate change. And governments will know their remaining carbon budgets – that is, how much carbon dioxide can still be emitted into the atmosphere while keeping global temperatures below agreed-to levels.

We have been working on greenhouse gas measurements for decades. In a new study, published Nov. 12, 2026, in the journal Science, we describe an alternative method for measuring these crucial carbon sinks, and what it shows.

We found that while the ocean sink has been expanding, meaning the oceans are taking in more carbon dioxide, that expansion might begin to slow down , leaving the oceans less effective at absorbing carbon in the coming decades. We found that the land sink has not been expanding, which was something of a surprise.
Measuring how much carbon is being taken up by the world’s oceans and forests is devilishly difficult and prohibitively expensive.

This is because many parts of the land and ocean don’t behave in the same ways. What occurs in one ocean region or forest can be very different from another; and the behavior in one year can be very different in the next, often for reasons scientists do not fully understand.

Computer models can help overcome some of these complexities, but they too have limitations. Satellites can also help, but they cannot see through clouds, nor can they see what is happening in the soil or mid-to-deep ocean.
As carbon cycle scientists, we set out to find a different way to measure these carbon sinks.

Our new study approaches the problem from another angle. We used high-precision measurements of atmospheric oxygen (O₂), combined with atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) measurements , to quantify how the ocean and land carbon sinks takeing up carbon dioxide.

This works because land, oceans and burning fossil fuels have different effects on oxygen: When fossil fuels are burned, they not only produce CO₂, they consume O₂. On land, when plants take up CO₂ to grow, they simultaneously release O₂. When the oceans take up atmospheric CO₂, there is no corresponding release of O₂.

This means that if we measure both CO₂ and O₂ in the atmosphere, then we can quantify the ocean and land carbon sinks. It is a straightforward mathematical approach of solving two equations with two unknowns, combined with our knowledge and measurements of the global budgets of CO₂ and O₂.
When we looked at the ocean and land carbon sinks over the past three decades, the results were surprising and sobering.

In contrast to most computer model simulations , we did not find the land carbon sink increasing over time to keep pace with increasing fossil fuel emissions. We did, however, find a larger ocean carbon sink than predicted by most models , and we found that it has been increasing as emissions grow.

If these trends in carbon sinks continue, then in the coming decades, humans will be relying more heavily on the oceans to slow down climate change. But in the next few decades, there are reasons to believe the oceans could become less effective at absorbing carbon.

For example, warmer waters are not able to hold as much gas , such as carbon dioxide. Warmer surface waters are also less efficient at mixing into the deep ocean , which has the beneficial effect of locking carbon dioxide away from the atmosphere for many hundreds of years.
The data for the past decade hints at the possibility that while the ocean carbon sink is increasing now, its rate of increase may be slowing down.

For the oceans, most computer models agree with each other, but, for the historical period, they do not match our oxygen-based results. For the land, models vary widely from each other, and most do not match our oxygen-based results.

Computer models are essential to provide governments with feasible scenarios to avoid dangerous climate change, but to be effective they need to be better grounded in what real-world observations are showing. Nature is difficult to represent with a series of equations, and observations are few considering the size of the planet.

We believe our study improves understanding of global carbon sinks and can help lead to more reliable projections of what might happen with climate change in the coming decades. But like any scientific approach, our oxygen method also has drawbacks.

The measurements themselves are challenging, such that only about 10 research laboratories in the world are routinely doing them. Calibrating the measurements is an ongoing challenge. Earth is not helping: Warmer waters hold less gas, meaning that as oceans warm in response to climate change, they expel some oxygen into the atmosphere . We must account for this in our carbon sink calculations. And to take into account variability in ocean circulation and other ocean processes, we have to average our results over 10-year time frames.

Policymakers and the public need answers faster . We believe the solution involves both improving the atmospheric oxygen approach and using other independent approaches: measurements of carbon and oxygen in the oceans, computer models and satellites are all essential. Combining these approaches will lead to more robust understanding of the carbon cycle and climate change, and better knowledge of where these valuable carbon sinks and the global climate are headed.

articles.title: To get Americans to care about climate change, just call it climate change
articles.author:
<name>Wändi Bruine de Bruin, Director of Behavioral Science & Policy Initiative, Schaeffer Institute of Public Policy & Government Service, USC Price School of Public Policy, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/wandi-bruine-de-bruin-275600"/>
paras: You may be hearing phrases like “climate crisis,” “climate emergency” and “climate justice” a lot as the 2026 United Nations climate summit is underway. Political leaders, including U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres , are using them to try to get across the urgent risks and consequences of climate change. The danger is real , but is using this language actually persuasive?

It turns out that Americans are more familiar with – and more concerned about – climate change and global warming than they are about climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice, according to a survey we conducted with a nationally representative sample of 5,137 Americans.
Moreover, we found no evidence that the alternative terms increased people’s sense of urgency, willingness to support climate-friendly policies or willingness to act.

The familiar terms – climate change and global warming – did at least as well, and sometimes better, than climate crisis and climate emergency in eliciting concern, perceived urgency and willingness to act. The phrase climate justice consistently tended to do worse, likely in part because it was the least familiar. These response patterns were similar among Republicans, Democrats and independents.
In our work as research psychologists , we have explored how Americans respond to the ways climate change is communicated and have uncovered a need to use straightforward language.

For example, people we interviewed for a study published in 2021 felt that climate experts were talking over their heads with terms like “adaptation,” “mitigation,” “sustainability” and “carbon-dioxide removal.” They wanted experts to use more familiar terms instead.

This inspired us to write a quick guide to climate jargon , published in The Conversation. Using everyday language makes information easier to understand, and even highly educated people tend to prefer it.

Jargon like “ biodiversity loss ” has similar problems. That refers to the shrinking variety of life on Earth, which is exacerbated by climate change. A survey of 7,338 U.S. adults led by one of us found people were much more familiar with and more concerned about “extinction of plants and animals” – or, if an explanation was provided, “nature loss”.

Even with an explanation, “biodiversity loss” was the least familiar and of least concern for people among several terms. Most people didn’t find “biodiversity crisis” or “extinction crisis” familiar either.
Yet, experts often use complex jargon because it is familiar to them, and they may not realize it is unfamiliar to others.

It has become common to talk about climate change and global warming as if they have the same meaning, but there are differences . Climate change refers to changes in the overall climate, while global warming refers specifically to rising temperatures.

A historical review found that, in the past, people were less likely to associate the term climate change with the idea that humans are actively warming the planet than they were with the term global warming. Perhaps this is why Democrats used to like the term global warming, while the popularization of the term climate change has been credited to Frank Luntz , an adviser to the George W. Bush administration.

Past surveys also found that Democrats used to think of global warming as being more serious than climate change, while Republicans thought of climate change as more serious than global warming. But according to a recent review , these partisan differences have now faded.

Alternative terms such as climate crisis, climate emergency and climate justice have been used to emphasize other aspects of climate change and to try to raise concern. In 2019, the British newspaper The Guardian switched to using climate crisis and climate emergency because it wanted to convey urgency.

Activists use the term climate justice to draw attention to climate change as a human rights challenge: Low-income people around the world suffer the most from the effects of climate change, despite being the least responsible for causing it.
Right now, the terms climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice are less familiar and elicit less concern than climate change or global warming.

Even if these terms become more commonplace, there is no guarantee that they will heighten concern or inspire action. In fact, studies have suggested that phrases like climate crisis could backfire if they don’t resonate with people.

Our advice: Don’t make the mistake of using overheated language. Just stick with familiar terms that people understand – use global warming when referring to rising temperatures and climate change for overall changes in the climate.
This updates an article originally published Aug. 12, 2024 , with a new study and discussions at the 2026 U.N. climate conference, COP31.

articles.title: Debate in New York City over city-run groceries is not just about food, but something bigger
articles.author:
<name>Nevin Cohen, Chair of the Department of Health Policy and Management, CUNY Graduate School of Public Health and Public Policy</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/nevin-cohen-1227050"/>
paras: New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow.

Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants . But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices.

Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers , supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses .

As a food policy scholar , I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs.

The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government . In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food.
It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see.

That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly.
If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide.
New York City has committed US$70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all.
While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices.
In this respect, the stores offer a “ public option ” – a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives , like public schools and city hospitals.

Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable.
At his May announcement , Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.”
Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses.

In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business.

A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program , known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods.
These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them.

FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers.

Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets.

This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare.
This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “ the submerged state .”
Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways.

First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food.

If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate.

Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable.

To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business.

Yet East Harlem’s Pathmark demonstrates that new supermarkets and smaller retailers can coexist. Between 2000 and 2015, the number of small grocery stores and bodegas in the neighborhood increased from 100 to 126 , while supermarkets rose from 10 to 18. That said, those figures don’t establish Pathmark’s effects on individual businesses.

The municipal stores’ impact on nearby retailers remains an open question. But the task for New York City is to ensure that private operators deliver excellent service and real savings, and that their commercial interests don’t undermine the public mission. It will also need to provide good working conditions and track effects on nearby businesses.
Ultimately, public ownership doesn’t guarantee success. But it makes government’s responsibility for the outcome impossible to miss.
Nevin Cohen receives research funding from the City of New York.

articles.title: MAHA suffered heavy losses in the 2026 midterms, but the movement is far from dead
articles.author:
<name>Robert Brehm, PhD Candidate in Politics, University of Virginia</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/robert-brehm-2776570"/>
paras: Candidates tied to the Make America Healthy Again, or MAHA, movement suffered a series of electoral defeats in the 2026 midterm elections, raising questions about MAHA’s political future.

Despite its name, MAHA has become a controversial force in American health politics. While the movement calls for healthier food , increased physical activity and greater corporate transparency, prominent figures within it have also challenged established scientific evidence, especially on vaccines .

Some commentators and critics have described the defeat of MAHA-aligned candidates like Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn as a “ brutal election night wipeout .” Others have asked whether MAHA is “ dying .”

Yet many Americans still support MAHA and the policies it champions . Its supporters also continue to hold powerful positions in the Trump administration – like Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya , and Kyle Diamantas , acting commissioner of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration – even as a new Congress prepares to take office in January 2027.

We are political scientists who study public opinion on healthcare policy . We see MAHA’s electoral losses as a political setback, not a death sentence. The movement’s influence extends beyond its candidates and the elections they contest.
MAHA’s electoral losses came amid a potentially generational swing toward Democrats across the country,

More than half the 24 gubernatorial and Congressional candidates endorsed by MAHA’s political action committee, MAHA Action , lost their election bids. These included Lahn, Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton and House candidate Vic Mellor in Rhode Island. Others, like incumbent Representative Anna Paulina Luna, R-FL, won by less than 1% in a district that she won by nearly 10 percentage points in 2024.

Lahn’s defeat stands out as a major loss. Lahn, a farmer who railed against pesticides on the campaign trail and promised to ban COVID-19 vaccinations in Iowa , was endorsed by Kennedy. Lahn has been described by some as a model MAHA candidate and received over US$1 million in campaign contributions from MAHA Action.

But the movement’s poor showing at the ballot box does not mean that some of MAHA’s ideas are unpopular among Americans. A May 2026 poll conducted by the health policy organization KFF found that 41% of American adults supported MAHA , including many Democrats and independents.

Many Americans also share MAHA’s concerns about food safety. According to KFF, 75% of Americans believe the government does too little to regulate chemical additives in food, while 64% say the same about agricultural pesticides.

Yet the popularity of MAHA policies did little to help MAHA-backed candidates win in the first election cycle where MAHA-aligned candidates were on the ballot. Following the midterm elections, some MAHA activists moved to blame President Donald Trump for failing to fulfill promises on these issues.

One prime example: In a postelection episode of Joe Rogan’s podcast, Calley Means, a former senior adviser to Kennedy, accused senior White House officials of allowing corporate interests to undermine MAHA’s goals. Dissatisfaction also spilled over to MAHA supporters in the general public, with one postelection poll finding that just over half of MAHA supporters feel the Trump administration made Americans’ health and well-being better throughout his second term in office.

Dissatisfaction with Trump, however, tells only part of the story. Another KFF poll conducted just before the election found that 42% of MAHA-supporting voters considered lowering healthcare costs their top health priority. By comparison, 21% prioritized restricting food additives, and 10% chose vaccine safety. Among voters more broadly, 55% believed Trump’s policies increased their healthcare costs, and 83% of those voters reported voting for Democrats. Most MAHA supporters, however, continued to vote for Republicans .

Supporting a movement, embracing its policy priorities and casting a ballot for its candidates do not necessarily go hand in hand. Americans can support MAHA’s goals without identifying with the movement or voting for its candidates. Likewise, MAHA supporters may vote Republican even when they are dissatisfied with Trump’s health policies. MAHA’s electoral losses, therefore, tell us little about how much support its ideas enjoy.

Despite its electoral losses, MAHA still holds considerable influence in Washington. Kennedy still leads HHS, where he can continue reshaping how the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention steers vaccine recommendations in a direction that aligns with his vaccine-skeptical views. These efforts face growing scrutiny amid public confusion over Kennedy’s vaccine guidance and reports that he sought to remove measles-related deaths from CDC statistics .

Kennedy appears undeterred by MAHA’s electoral setbacks. Following the election, he praised incoming White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller , declaring, “Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken.”

MAHA’s continued influence in the Trump administration, however, will face new obstacles now that Democrats control Congress. Facing greater opposition, the administration may increasingly rely on executive actions, including executive orders , new federal regulations and agency reports , to advance its health policies. However, Congress can also investigate HHS decisions and use its control over federal spending to limit what the agency can do.

MAHA’s political future remains uncertain. Some supporters may gradually move toward Democrats, particularly those concerned about corporate influence, pharmaceutical industry accountability and food safety. These concerns cross partisan lines , giving Democrats an opportunity to appeal to voters dissatisfied with Trump but still supportive of MAHA’s priorities.

MAHA could also become a movement independent of Trump and MAGA. It could bring together Americans who care about health and wellness, distrust major institutions and oppose corporate influence over food and medicine. Kennedy’s independent presidential campaign attracted as much as 15% support among voters in July 2024. This showed that an alternative to the two major parties could attract substantial support.

Whether MAHA remains tied to Trump’s increasingly divided coalition will shape its future beyond his presidency. The frustrations and health concerns that fueled its rise among Americans have not disappeared.
