articles.title: Republican gerrymandering worked pretty well in Texas and Florida, even if it backfired in North Carolina and Ohio
articles.author:
<name>Charlie Hunt, Associate Professor of Political Science, Boise State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/charlie-hunt-1364391"/>
paras: During the 2026 election cycle, Republicans enacted a series of gerrymanders – a form of partisan redistricting – in a handful of states to give them a disproportionate edge over Democrats in their congressional delegations. Democrats responded with a successful redistricting effort in California and an unsuccessful one in Virginia .
Gerrymandering has obvious implications for fairness and democracy, characterized by some as politicians picking their voters, not voters picking their politicians.
There’s also a practical consideration for those doing the gerrymandering: The efforts can fail when they overplay their hand.

By spreading their supportive voters across many districts, parties can create more seats that may lean in their direction. But if spread too thin, these efforts can backfire and net seats for the other party, particularly in a “wave” election year that favors the other party. This unintended consequence is often referred to as a “dummymander .”
So, with such massive Democratic majorities poised to enter the 120th Congress, did Republican attempts to gerrymander actually end up costing them some seats in the U.S. House?
The answer isn’t as clear-cut as you might think.

Republican state legislatures in Ohio and North Carolina redrew their congressional maps in 2025 , crafting a set of districts they believed would maximize the number of seats they could win in the House.

Despite both states being traditionally competitive in statewide elections, their state legislatures drew a collection of seats Republicans believed they would win: 12 of these 15 new seats in Ohio and 11 out of 14 in North Carolina included a majority of voters who voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

But in 2026, Democrats across the country won dozens of seats that had previously seemed out of reach, including districts Trump won by double digits in 2024. Many of these seats were in heavily gerrymandered Republican seats.

In Ohio and North Carolina, the size and scope of the midterm backlash against Trump and his party put many of the seats Republicans targeted in these states, including ones Trump won by as many as 20 points, in serious jeopardy.
In the end, the Democratic wave overcame so many Trump-won seats in these states that their new delegations to Congress may be more Democratic than they would have been without the gerrymanders.

Texas and Florida also targeted a series of Democrat-held seats to flip their way in 2026. Nine such seats across these two states, as well as a vulnerable seat held by Democratic U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures in Alabama, were the targets of gerrymanders that created new districts that Trump won in 2024, all by 9 percentage points or more.

But once the 2026 Democratic wave swept through the deep South, these gerrymanders were essentially canceled out. Despite the gains the party projected, Republicans in these three states appear likely to enter the 120th Congress with delegations the same size as they had in the 119th.

Other Republican gerrymandering attempts were successful, but only barely. In Tennessee’s 9th District, the last remaining Democratic seat in the state was gerrymandered into a district Donald Trump won by 21 points in 2024. Republicans did hold that seat as expected, but only by 2,500 votes, or just over 1 percentage point.
Many of these gerrymanders were not maximally successful. But were they true dummymanders?
In North Carolina and Ohio it does appear that Republicans overplayed their hand by counting on past Trump voters in a national environment that proved so favorable to the Democrats.

In Ohio, a gerrymander that aimed for a two-thirds Republican majority in their House delegation will net them less than half of that in the 120th Congress . That outcome ended up producing a more representative result, one that was roughly in line with the two parties’ 2026 popular vote shares in the state.

North Carolina was a more drastic dummymander: The Republicans aimed to design districts where they would win seats accounting for almost two-thirds of their congressional delegation. But the party is currently poised to hold , at best, less than one-third of their state’s seats.

And California, which Democrats gerrymandered in reaction to Republican efforts in other states, is a partisan success story . The state is projected to send only 8% of their delegation to the House as Republicans, despite voting 30% for Republicans statewide.

In Texas and Florida the story is more complicated. Democrats in those states retained most of the seats they held that their Republican legislatures targeted in their gerrymanders, thanks to historic shifts by Hispanic voters who had voted for Trump in the 2024 election.

But gerrymanders can be effective beyond marginal, targeted districts. Taken as a whole, Texas’ and Florida’s district boundaries were drawn so favorably for Republicans that even a Democratic tsunami managed only to keep these states’ delegations identical in the next Congress, since many other districts remained safe for Republicans.

In these states, Republicans still enjoy a greater proportion of House seats than their popular vote margins would reflect. And in a less Democrat-leaning election cycle, many of these gerrymandered seats could very well shift back toward Republicans.

As poor as the outcome of the 2026 midterms was for Republicans, it could have been even worse. In fact, some Republican states might count themselves lucky that their attempts to gerrymander failed in the lead-up to the midterms.

In traditionally Republican states such as Missouri and Utah , courts struck down gerrymanders that would have created a series of districts that Trump won by around 20 percentage points . If the gerrymanders had not been struck down, Democrats’ shocking success in similar districts across the country could have netted them as many as five additional seats in these states.

A similar situation played out in Indiana and South Carolina . New maps pushed by Trump that failed in their state legislatures were intended to produce even more lopsided Republican gains. But analysis from the Cook Political Report found that these maps might have netted Democrats as many as six out of South Carolina’s seven House seats, and eight out of Indiana’s nine. Instead, Democrats seem likely to end up with only a pair of seats in each state.
The 2026 election cycle demonstrates that gerrymandering is a far more complex and dynamic proposition than it is often treated by pundits and parties.

Wave elections of this size can often overcome the intended effects of gerrymandered maps, but subsequent elections might find them much more effective. Plus, parties often draw gerrymandered maps based on the previous election’s presidential results – a measure that may be less reliable as voters continue to make more unexpected choices.

Moreover, both red and blue states are dealing with the aftermath of the Louisiana v. Callais Supreme Court decision , which made the gerrymandering of racial groups easier to do without court interventions. Over the next two years, Republicans may attempt to implement even more new maps in many new states, particularly in the South. Those new districts will likely aim to dilute majority-Black districts that are no longer protected by the Voting Rights Act.
Meanwhile, Democratic state governments appear poised to continue with their pushback against last cycle’s Republican efforts with gerrymanders of their own over the next two years.
But the Republican redistricting failures of the 2026 cycle, including their near misses, should make both parties cautious about future attempts.

articles.title: OfferUp co-founder sees ‘mini power plants’ in buildings full of EVs
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Nick Huzar co-founded Juicer Energy in 2023 to make electric vehicle charging more widespread and reliable. Now the Seattle-area startup is pursuing a broader goal: helping buildings manage rising electricity demand and costs.

Juicer installs and operates EV charging systems at apartment buildings, hotels and other properties. It is also developing battery systems to store electricity on-site and help manage the power needed for charging and other building uses.

The push comes as data centers and the growing use of electricity for transportation, heating and other needs put more pressure on the grid. Batteries can help balance supply and demand by storing energy when electricity is plentiful and releasing it when demand peaks. In some cases, they can reduce the need for costly grid upgrades or new power plants built to meet peak demand.
“We think there’s a big opportunity there,” Huzar said. He spoke at an event this week hosted by GeekWire and Bank of America at the Bellevue showroom of Ferrari of Seattle.

Other companies are similarly pairing EV charging with battery storage. Fellow Seattle startup Electric Era has deployed battery-backed fast chargers at retailers including Costco and convenience stores. ADS-TEC Energy and XCharge also sell fast-charging systems with integrated batteries.

Huzar, OfferUp’s co-founder and former CEO, sees an opportunity to make buildings more self-sufficient by combining hardware and energy-management software. He said Juicer has a project scheduled to come online in 2027 with 70 chargers in one building.
His longer-term vision also includes tapping the energy stored in vehicles connected to those buildings.
“Imagine you’re an apartment owner and you have 20 EVs, 40 EVs plugged in,” Huzar said. “That is a huge amount of power. Like you’re a mini power plant at that point.”

He described feeding excess electricity back to the grid as a possibility that remains years away. He also predicted that most businesses, apartments and homes would have on-site batteries within the next decade, in part because battery costs continue to fall.
Juicer started with EV charging, Huzar said, “but the more we’ve gotten into this, the more we realize that we actually can build an asset for buildings versus relying on the grid.”

articles.title: Amazon tops Forbes’ list of America’s best companies, edging out Apple for No. 1
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Amazon is the best company in America, according to Forbes.
The Seattle tech giant took the No. 1 spot on the publication’s 2027 “America’s Best Companies” list, moving up from No. 2 last year and edging out Apple.
Three other Washington state companies landed in the top 50: Microsoft at No. 6, Costco at No. 13 and Alaska Air Group at No. 39.

Last year’s No. 1, Berkshire Hathaway, slipped to No. 4. Nvidia ranked No. 3 on the same day CEO Jensen Huang resigned, following his admission of an extramarital affair. JPMorganChase, Alphabet, Royal Caribbean Group, Walmart and Marriott International round out the top 10.

Now in its third year, the ranking scores thousands of the largest public and private U.S. companies on factors including customer and employee sentiment, financial performance, creditworthiness, cybersecurity and innovation. Forbes said it worked with 12 data organizations to build the index.

Forbes said Amazon’s financial strength and size, its standing in news and social media, and the range of voices across the company and its leadership lifted it to No. 1. Apple scored especially well on employee satisfaction, customer loyalty, financial strength and innovation.
Forbes also pointed to Amazon’s speed, citing a feature that lets customers shop by text message. An employee suggested it in October and it launched Nov. 6.

“Innovating for customers, doing it fast, working backwards from their needs, that’s really at our core,” Beth Galetti, Amazon’s senior vice president of people, experience and technology, told Forbes.
In its own blog post Thursday, Amazon highlighted everything from faster delivery and custom AI chips to warehouse robotics and higher pay for frontline workers.

The ranking comes after a year of workforce cuts at Amazon. The company eliminated about 30,000 corporate jobs in rounds announced in October 2025 and January 2026, including more than 4,500 in Washington state. Smaller cuts followed throughout the year, including layoffs of fewer than 1,000 corporate employees in October, mainly in its Stores unit.

articles.title: XML pioneer Jean Paoli’s startup Docugami acquired by Inveniam after open-source partnership
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Docugami , the Seattle-area startup led by XML co-creator Jean Paoli, has been acquired by Inveniam , a Detroit-area company that uses blockchain to help investors verify the data behind assets such as commercial real estate and private loans.
The deal follows a partnership this summer in which the companies released DGML , Docugami’s open-source format for turning business documents into data that AI agents can use and check.

Financial terms of the acquisition weren’t disclosed. All of Docugami’s employees are joining Inveniam, a Docugami spokesperson said. The team numbers about 50 including contractors. Paoli becomes Inveniam’s chief product and technology officer, and Docugami will keep operating from Kirkland, according to the announcement .
Paoli co-founded Docugami in 2018 after more than 20 years at Microsoft, where he helped create XML and the Office file formats.

The startup, based in Kirkland, Wash., raised a $10 million seed round in 2020 led by SignalFire, with backing from Bob Muglia, the former Microsoft executive and Snowflake CEO. Grammarly, the writing-assistant company now known as Superhuman, later disclosed that it had taken part in the round, its first investment in another company .
Prior to the acquisition, Docugami ranked No. 155 on the GeekWire 200 , our list of the Pacific Northwest’s top independent, privately held startups.

DGML labels each piece of a document by what it is — a base rent, a loan payment, a liability cap — so a single figure can be traced back to the page it came from. Inveniam records a digital fingerprint of each of those data points on its blockchain, called NVNM Chain, so any later change shows up.

Inveniam executives said Thursday morning on a livestream with Paoli that DGML solves a problem they’ve had in bringing on new clients: every client’s documents are different, which required templates and standard formats before the data could be used.
“One promise I want to make personally: DGML stays open and its openness is strategic to Inveniam,” Paoli wrote in a LinkedIn post .

Inveniam, led by CEO Patrick O’Meara, also acquired Mantra , a crypto company that provided the original technology for NVNM Chain, earlier this year. Mantra co-founder John Patrick Mullin said on the livestream that NVNM Chain will move to its own independent blockchain, with the main network expected to launch in the next few weeks.
Fees on that network will help fund buybacks of an NVNM cryptocurrency token, Mullin said. O’Meara proposed a separate session on when that token will launch.

articles.title: Bellevue Council Settles On 10-Year Transportation Funding Plan
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The Bellevue City Council has signed off on a plan to add more than $100 million in transportation funding over the next decade, utilizing a dedicated 0.1% bump in the city's sales tax rate. The spend plan for that money ramps up the pace of spending on bicycle and pedestrian projects by nearly 40%, but also invests heavily in big-ticket items including several pricey intersection expansions and a new roadway project through BelRed that has proven divisive.

With an additional $33 million expected to flow into city coffers through 2036, Bellevue would advance 37 projects to improve bike and pedestrian infrastructure, five more than had been planned previously. Those include multimodal upgrades to 108th Avenue NE, pedestrian improvements along Main Street in Old Bellevue, and design funds for a connection to Eastrail near Main Street in Wilburton.
Plus, the number of neighborhood safety projects intended to calm vehicle traffic would jump from 33 to 46 thanks to an additional $13.2 million investment.

Bellevue would also invest an additional $18.9 million in projects intended to improve traffic flow, including $14 million to widen two intersections – NE 12th St at 116th Avenue NE, and SE 8th Street at 114th Avenue SE – and another $4.45 million for partial intersection changes at 148th Avenue NE and NE 8th Street. Those three projects alone represent 30% more spending than the planned increase for neighborhood mobility.

Advancing walking, biking, and safety upgrades for all users while at the same time chasing the dream of free-flowing traffic – a priority of the Bellevue Chamber of Commerce and other business leaders – illustrates Bellevue's current political reality, stuck in a liminal space between suburb and city. That reality has manifested in other ways this year, including a reluctance to follow other major Washington cities in rethinking things like parking mandates .

Over the past few weeks, the funding proposal has been walked back slightly compared to earlier iterations. A $20 vehicle license fee that would have been paired with the sales tax bump has been dropped; instead, the City will allocate $8 million in one-time funding toward neighborhood safety projects that would have been funded with those dollars.
The council rejected a motion made by Jared Nieuwenhuis at its November 3 meeting to send the package to voters next April, citing a clear need to make these investments in transportation.

"We have heard from residents who are concerned about the cost of living, and we have also heard from people who have been waiting years for safer streets, sidewalks, and better transportation," Mayor Mo Malakoutian said. "And both concerns are real, and we should take them seriously. And we also need to look at where Bellevue is heading. We are planning for 35,000 more homes and 70,000 more jobs by 2044, and we are already seeing that growth take shape, in Wilburton. Since we updated the zoning last year, we have seen application for more than 2,300 new homes in just that one neighborhood, and that is exactly why we need to act now. Transportation projects take years to plan, design, and build. If we wait until those homes are built and traffic get worse, we have waited too long."

A full third of the new dollars – $37 million – will be used to get the Spring Boulevard Zone 3 project completed, a connection that City leaders see as essential to future growth in and around the BelRed and Spring District growth centers. As an alternative to the high-speed arterial that is BelRed Road, the new street will come with separated bike lanes and sidewalks in addition to one vehicle travel lane in each direction. But the eye-popping $74 million price tag has left sour taste in many Bellevue residents' mouths, urbanist or not.

The new stretch of Spring Boulevard will cut directly through one of the only new parks planned in the area, and the dollars lavished on this project could potentially be leveraged to achieve bigger citywide gains in bike and pedestrian access, in the wake of the full pivot away from the ambitious quick-build Bike Bellevue plan in 2024.

Councilmember Vishal Bhargava also framed the need to ramp up transportation spending as being directly tied to planned growth, roping in the issue of safety. That has been a major topic of conversation at the council for most of this year, in the wake of three deaths and 38 serious injuries occurring on Bellevue's roadways in 2025 – the highest rate in 10 years.

"I think there is a need for us to take action to match the development of transportation infrastructure to keep pace with the growth that we have bolstered in the city, through things like middle housing, the comprehensive plan re-densification in many areas, even the economic development efforts that we're putting in to bring jobs into the city," Bhargava said. "We need to make transportation investments to keep pace. Otherwise, we're going to struggle not just from a mobility standpoint, and more importantly, from a safety standpoint."

But even as the plan tries to please everyone, some Bellevue residents pushed to scale back the investments in walking and biking to spend more on congestion reduction. On council, it was Nieuwenhuis who gave voice to the idea that the plan was weighted too far away from cars, asking to see a breakdown of exact levels of spending for bikes versus pedestrians.

"I don't know how much we're putting towards either one of those right now, and it's challenging because, as the mayor rightly said, we are experiencing growth," Nieuwenhuis said. "I don't think the growth is going to happen quite as quickly, but we are experiencing growth. But we are spending almost like 70% more on bike and ped than we are in [the] vehicle [category]. So how are we going to adjust for that growth, be able to get cars, trucks, first responders, etc., through the city, if we are putting more of our emphasis on bikes than we are on vehicles."
In his response to Nieuwenhuis, Bellevue Transportation Director Andrew Singelakis framed the city's bike infrastructure as long neglected.

"There's a significant amount of money that's in there as well for the vehicle mode that needs to be addressed as well," Singelakis said. "But I think that really we're so far behind in the bike mode that making connections and having those connections occur will end up enhancing that system."

Another major factor that is limiting Bellevue's ability to satisfy calls to improve congestion is the high expense of car projects compared to bike and pedestrian ones, a fact that will only become more pronounced as the city continues to densify.

"As we're thinking about the available land for roadway infrastructure, there are very few spaces left to add vehicle capacity, and that's part of the reason why you're seeing such an emphasis on completing that system with access to transit, with bike and ped, because it's building on the existing capacity to make sure that the roads function well and provide a full network," John Resha, Bellevue's Chief Financial Officer, said. "We're kind of in that space of, we're now a little heavier weighted in the multimodal side because of that constraint of the land, [it] just isn't available to build more roadways."

Some councilmembers voiced support for retaining the $20 car tab, a funding source that would have freed up some general fund dollars, but also allowed Bellevue to complete three more neighborhood mobility projects. Additionally, car tab funding could have added one more bicycle and pedestrian project to the workplan, a multimodal study on Main Street between 100th and 108th Avenue NE.

"I think that for the families who have two working parents that have to be to work before school starts, they have to pay for childcare, and if their children can walk to school from their home, that's a cost saving for them, if it's safe. And that's a reality for a lot of families in Bellevue," Councilmember Lynne Robinson said. "Also, we're retiring a parks levy in two years, and so that's going to be I think almost $50 that people will not be paying if we do not re-up it."

While the new funding source will start to flow in mid-2027, the 10-year plan won't actually be set in stone; so, there is the potential for a reassessment of the project list sometime down the road. The intersection expansion at SE 8th and 114th, for example, won't start design until 2031, according to the City's current plans. The widening of 148th Avenue NE and NE 8th Street would be designed at the same time, but not start construction until 2036.

"The council will have the opportunity, with staff support and help, to revisit the prioritization of these projects as we get additional information on safety impacts, congestion changes, behavior changes, and across modes," Bhargava said. "The modal split can change, and different things can become more important from a safety and connectivity standpoint."
A final vote to approve Bellevue's 2027-2028 budget, including the 0.1% sales tax increase, is set for the November 17 meeting.

articles.title: Wilson Makes First Veto As Mayor Count, Tweaking RV Parking Reform
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: Four members of the Seattle City Council chose to uphold Mayor Katie Wilson’s first veto in her tenure as mayor, with Councilmember Rob Saka flipping his original council vote. Overturning the veto council would have required a two-thirds council majority – six votes.

Last week, Wilson held a press conference to announce she was vetoing Councilmember Dan Strauss’s bill that would have instituted a recreational vehicle (RV) permitting program with the goal of ultimately removing all RVs from Seattle’s streets. Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck and Saka flanked Wilson in a show of support.
Wilson signed the other bills in Strauss’s RV package.

“As the Mayor, it is my responsibility to ensure that our city policies and programs are feasible, are a cost-effective use of public resources, and have a reasonable likelihood of achieving their stated goals,” Wilson said at her press conference. “I vetoed this bill because I'm concerned that the permit program outlined in Council Bill 121283 does not meet that threshold, and I wanted to give the council an opportunity to consider an alternative pathway.”

Wilson laid out that alternative pathway for helping people living in their RVs at the press conference and signed an executive order to formalize her intentions. Wilson’s plan involves strengthening outreach and services for people living in RVs, including providing resources for service providers to help connect folks to RV safe lots, shelter options, and other services, to include the opening of Glassyards Commons, a combination of RV safe lot and tiny house village, later this month.

Wilson intends to include RV residents in the citywide by-name list that features in her new strategy for addressing homelessness, and she also expressed interest in learning how RVs are being used, including by those people who aren’t living in them or might be traveling for work, medical care, or in order to do caretaking.

The executive order also forms a working group that will bring together City departments and community partners to focus specifically on the neighborhood impacts and public safety issues that involve RVs in Seattle.

Earlier in the summer, Strauss had introduced a package of legislation he framed as designed to help people living in their RVs. The package included opening a new RV safe lot and providing RV storage for people who were interested in keeping their RVs while trying a housing option, in addition to the restrictive permitting program targeted by the veto, which opponents said would simply increase the number of unhoused people on Seattle’s streets.
Strauss’s permitting program wasn’t set to take effect until April 2027, which he said would give the City time to make any necessary changes.

“This time is incredibly important for understanding what rules have changed, for hearing, digesting, and learning about the concerns that we've heard from some today, to ensure that if we need to change this legislation before the April effective date that we're able to,” Strauss said before the original vote.

The Seattle City Council passed Strauss’s package of legislation on October 20, with the legislation creating the permitting program passing on a 6-3 vote. The three councilmembers from the progressive wing – Councilmembers Dionne Foster, Eddie Lin, and Alexis Mercedes Rinck — voted against the bill. Passing the bill with a 6-3 majority seemed to promise Strauss a veto-proof majority to ensure his proposal became law.
However, the six votes weren’t as firm as Strauss had thought.

Wilson laid out several concerns relating to the RV permitting program that she said ultimately caused her to change her mind on supporting it. The program as described in the legislation would have been complex, involving several departments as well as requiring the hiring of several new positions and containing ongoing enforcement responsibilities. Strauss insisted that the census of people living in RVs be only one time so as to not attract people from other places living in their RVs to Seattle, but such a census would be difficult to undertake while ignoring all future Seattle residents who might end up someday living in an RV.

The potential cost of the program was a concern in Seattle’s current tight budget environment. The City estimated that implementing the permitting program could cost more than $10 million, a number Strauss contested.

Other issues mentioned by Wilson included the legal risk to which the legislation might expose the City, the possibility the program would pull capacity away from other urgent public safety issues, and the risk that the program might actually increase unsheltered homelessness, as some advocates had been contending.
Rinck didn’t mince words in her speech supporting Wilson’s decision to veto.

“I am here today in full support of Mayor Wilson's action. She is vetoing a permit program that is harmful, costly, and impossible to implement, one that won't deliver on what it promises,” Rinck said. “She's issuing an executive order that will actually help move people out of RVs and into shelter and housing while addressing problematic and criminal activity. Seattle residents deserve a government that's honest about what a policy can do and can't do. When we pass a law, they expect it to work. They expect it to be enforceable, and they expect it to be worth what it costs them. A permit program that we can't staff, can't enforce, and can't pay for does not meet that standard.”
Wilson waited until the last possible day to use her veto power, with Saka changing his mind on his vote at the eleventh hour, demolishing the council’s veto-proof majority.

“I’ve heard from the Mayor about unreasonable expectations, the ability or or lack thereof of our City to actually implement something like this on such an ambitious timeline,” Saka said. “But more importantly, I heard a framework for an alternative proposal, an alternative solution that could potentially be stronger, more effective, [and] bring more people along. That's why I welcome the Mayor's initiative, and believe we should give this process a fair opportunity to succeed.”
Saka said he hadn’t viewed Wilson’s executive order until the night before she announced her veto.

Strauss complained that Wilson had agreed to sign his entire legislative package into law, and that it had been delayed this year because he had put her legislative priorities ahead of his own. Strauss also said that a work group was already a part of his legislation so changes could be made ahead of implementation.

“I feel like [Wilson’s] word has been disingenuous,” Strauss said at a press conference. “There have been a number of times that she's broken the promises that she's made to me or the commitments that she's made to me, and that's why I say I can't trust her word anymore. It's not just one interaction. It's been several, and it's been a pattern over time.”
Wilson told the press, however, that she had simply changed her mind upon receiving more information.

“I was not originally intending to veto this legislation, and before the passage of the legislation, my staff communicated to Councilmember Strauss that I did not have a plan to veto it, which was absolutely true at that time,” Wilson said. “Since then, as my thinking has shifted and I got into more of a posture of considering all options, we were also transparent in communicating that to his office.”

Alison Eisinger, the executive director of the Seattle/King County Coalition on Homelessness, said in a public comment this morning that over 4,700 letters had been sent urging the council to uphold the veto.

“This legislation, this specific piece of legislation of the six brought forward, is a ban,” Eisinger said. “The changes to parking rules and the permit program would have created a draconian ban on hundreds of people who live in the best shelter available to them. Voting to uphold the veto will demonstrate that together with all of us, you're committed to a Seattle where we work together to strengthen our community, resolve problems, and create a better housed future.”

When discussing the council vote on the veto, Strauss said he shared the concerns about the implementation of the RV permitting program, but that his legislation would allow them to get around a table and find solutions. Strauss didn’t explain why he didn’t address more of his own concerns before bringing his legislation forward for council passage.
Saka reiterated his desire to give Wilson’s plan a chance.

“In my view, we need more leaders at all levels of government to humble themselves if and when new information becomes available, and to make the best decision, do the greatest good for the greatest number,” Saka said.

“To say that a vote today to sustain the veto is a vote for a new path is duplicitous, in my opinion, because that report can be provided even before the check and adjust period is halfway over,” Strauss shot back.
Later in the meeting, Councilmember Eddie Lin pointed out this comment might be against council rules.

“I do believe we have a rule about not impugning motives of each other, and I just heard something about intent being duplicitous, and I just want to address that because I do think that it is impugning the motive of one of my colleagues,” Lin said.

“I, too, took some issue with some comments made towards the very end of this conversation, and you know, the Seattle passive aggressive, subtle slights, let's disagree on the merits,” Saka said. “Councilmember Strauss, you have a problem with me? I promise you, I'm not the one. You can take it up with me directly.”
Hollingsworth expressed her disappointment in the performance of the King County Regional Homelessness Authority and explained why she was still voting in support of Strauss’s bill.

“We cannot place all the challenges on Mayor Wilson and this administration. This has been going on for years, for years,” Hollingsworth said. “But I do believe that we have to move beyond intentions and focus on executions. So I do respect folks that come, I do respect that my colleagues have different perspective on this legislation, but I also believe that when we raise concerns about potential harms of a policy, we must equally be willing to confront the harm that is happening under the status quo. That is what's important.”

With the RV permitting program no longer set to move forward, Wilson will be convening her working group to look more closely at issues involving RVs. Strauss said he’ll expect a report from the group by January 15.

Meanwhile, Strauss still has to complete his duties as Budget Chair, with the council set to make their final budget vote on November 20. Strauss complained that upholding this veto will impact that budget plan, requiring changes to his balancing package presented last week.

articles.title: Katie Wilson Headlines Speaker Lineup for The Urbanist's Dec. 4 Holiday Party

paras: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and newly elected State Representative Jessica Forsythe are headlining the speaking program for our Winter Holiday Party on December 4 !

articles.title: Gyeok and its delicious Korean chicken noodle soup next for former Capitol Hill fine dining space
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A Broadway restaurant space previously home to some of the finest neighborhood dining of the past decade is ready to hatch a new venture that represents a twist of two seemingly indomitable Capitol Hill dining trends.

The former home of five-star — and $$$$$ — Altura is being readied to become Gyeok , a new sibling restaurant to Broadway’s Busan Jeong , the Korean joint from global restaurateur Hoyeon Park that opened earlier this year on the east side of the street specializing in “Korean Pork Broth Rice” with savory soups, Korean dumplings, Korean pancakes, and specialties like blood sausage.

Another ripple in the wave of Korean-inspired openings is one thing but Park tells CHS Gyeok will also be part of another food and drink trend quickly changing the menus of Capitol Hill dining — chicken.
As with Busan Jeong’s focus around rich broth, Gyeok will specialize in Korean chicken kalguksu — “knife-cut noodle soup,” Park writes — and the Korean ginseng chicken soup samgye-tang.
There is a third trend in the mix, of course. The across the street opening will help the Gyeok and Busan teams with logistics and easy supply runs.

Altura and its sibling restaurant Carrello enjoyed a similar relationship until chef/owner Nathan Lockwood decided to move Altura across the street to take over the Carrello space this fall. After starting 15 years ago on the west side of Broadway, Altura now continues its award-winning tasting menu service while adding some Carrello touches in the much larger space on the east side.

We don’t know if Altura is serving any chicken these days but the rest of Capitol Hill sure is. CHS reported earlier this week on yet another new chicken joint opening up — Rizzo’s Crispy Chicken is taking shape next door to Dick’s Drive-in and part of a flock of new chicken-centered ventures now taking roost around Capitol Hill and the Central District.

Meanwhile, Korean food and drink has become a major component of the dining scene — with a little help from the yes-it-really-exists Korean Food Promotion Institute . As CHS wrote last year, knowing your way around a Korean spice rack is pretty useful on Capitol Hill. The Gol Mok Korean Market Bar holds down a space on E Pike . Yeobo Cafe and Bar and its Korean-American comfort food on E Madison is another addition. Another new joint , Seoul Mates , opened in a former sushi bar at 10th and Union. At the core, MEET BBQ from Heong Soon Park has grown into a center of the scene on E Pike.
The Chicken Food Promotion Institute could not be reached for comment.
Hoyeon Park tells CHS he is planning for Gyeok and its delicious Korean chicken noodle soup to debut in early December.
Gyeok will open soon at 617 Broadway E. Follow @gyeok.seattle for updates.

articles.title: Maintenance of automated trains
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: Sound Transit has recently reduced construction cost with smaller station designs (for example Alaska Junction) but their current four-car trains are 380ft long while Vancouver’s SkyTrains are only 280ft long. That still requires bigger, harder to locate, and more expensive stations. Due to automation SkyTrain can operate more frequently and therefore still handle higher ridership while providing higher convenience. Sound Transit has considered automation but is concerned about interoperability with current trains. They could add an operator on surface portions such as through Rainier Valley. If they would keep the Ballard line separate, then interoperability would not be an issue, but Sound Transit would need to worry about where to park them at night (“stabling”), clean them, and maintain them. When Sound Transit considered a starter line for Ballard, they concluded that they would need to build an operations and maintenance facility (OMF) in Interbay and that its cost would offset all savings. I gathered some ideas on how to potentially reduce such effort.

If you connect the Ballard (starter) line with the main line, you could still use the existing Central OMF in SODO. If such a connection is not feasible, then you could build a separate regular OMF or consider other options.

For maintenance, you could connect to the BNSF tracks at Interbay and SODO to move trains between the Ballard line and the SODO OMF during off-hours. As BNSF tracks are not electrified, you would need a separate locomotive to pull the trains. You could also truck the trains as these occasional maintenance events.
For nightly cleaning and monthly maintenance, you may still want a separate small cleaning center just like SeaTac airport cleans their people movers locally.

When Lynnwood Link opened, Sound Transit did not have enough stabling space at the Central OMF. They parked some trains at various stations at night . Operators had to pick them up there in the morning and park them there at night. Automated trains may operate through the night. If you do not want to operate through the night to maintain the tracks, you can park automated trains anywhere. They can wake themselves up in the morning, go through safety checks, and move to the first station by themselves. In fact, if Sound Transit wants to reduce service in the evening and start cleaning cars, they could send them to the OMF for daily cleaning and afterwards park them at any pocket track. If they want to reduce service further, they even reduce service to a single track towards the end of the line and use the other track for stabling.
This would reduce the size and cost of the OMF considerably. As automated trains can move (“shunting”) themselves in and out of the OMF, there is no need for shunting staff.
Sound Transit could even allow construction of transit-oriented housing above such facility as the Hong Kong MTA has done for example.
If Ballard trains don’t need to use the Central OMF in SODO, Sound Transit may be able to reduce the size of the Everett OMF. This may shift some of the cost.

I would hope by reducing the cost of the maintenance facility, Sound Transit would consider an automated Ballard starter line and shorter stations. Due to its lower cost, it could connect Ballard sooner and also be more attractive to riders due to its higher frequency and longer service hours.

articles.title: Will Silicon Valley Survive the Death of MAGA?
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: This weekend, the Bainbridge Island Film Festival presents Ghost in the Machine— a documentary whose value has been significantly increased by the results of last week’s midterm elections. Directed, written, and produced by Valerie Veatch (who was interviewed by The Stranger in May), the film concerns the origins of artificial intelligence, which the film traces back to 19th century eugenics, a project that provided no insights on the nature and structure of human mental capacities but simply justified the colonial (and therefore racist) expansion of European capital.

The documentary also explores the rise and economic mythologizing of Silicon Valley, the environmental impact of data centers, the exploitation of Black African immaterial labor (particularly in countries colonized by the British), and the first half of Trump’s second term in office, which has been defined by a very close alliance between Big Tech and the White House.

Though shot and composed 2025, Ghost in the Machine throws a very bright light on recent post-election events. This week, the CEO of the Silicon Valley-based corporation Nvidia, Jensen Huang, resigned because of an extramarital affair with a woman, Alice Huang, reported to be a Chinese spy . But what makes this spectacular scandal relevant to the issues explored in the late parts of the documentary is that Nvidia donated $25 million to Trump’s big and not beautiful ballroom (it will be torn down as soon as he leaves office ) in exchange for regulations that permitted “the sale of advanced AI chips to China.”

What’s revealing here is not the Bond-hot corporate espionage (wine in spiffy restaurants, flights in private jets, and so on), or the transformation of a big chunk of the White House into an elaborate bribe scheme, but how the intimate relationship between Trump and Silicon Valley lost much of its steam after MAGA collapsed on November 3, 2026. Watch Ghost in the Machine , which, to be honest is too short (it needed the length of Ken Burns The Vietnam War : 18 hours), and it becomes very clear why Musk gave MAGA a mind-breaking $445 million for the midterm elections . For him and his class of billionaires, this expenditure was a matter of life and death. Where will Silicon Valley go after MAGA?

As for Sam Altman, no dream, no matter how feverish, could match the nuttiness of his business model: We need to invest big in AI so it can be powerful enough to figure out how to make money on this big investment. And that’s where we find ourselves after the election. Do not miss this documentary.
See Ghost in the Machine November 13, 1:30 pm at Lynwood Theatre and November 14 at1:45 pm at Bainbridge Cinemas. Visit Brainbridge Island Film Festival for information about other films.

articles.title: Wilson Greenlights Expansion of Surveillance in Seattle
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: On Tuesday, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson announced that the City will be immediately moving forward with the expansion of the Seattle Police Department’s (SPD’s) surveillance program that was approved by city council last fall.

To assist her in this decision, Wilson engaged the New York University (NYU) Policing Project to perform a governance audit assessing the civil rights and liberties risks posed by SPD’s surveillance program, including their real-time crime center, CCTV cameras, and Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) cameras. Wilson said the City plans to implement many of the recommendations outlined in the report.
NYU didn’t assess the civil liberties risks of Seattle’s automated license plate readers due to their usage being suspended earlier in the year to comply with a new state law .

During her campaign, Wilson ran on an anti-surveillance platform, and at the beginning of her term, activists asked her to turn off all of SPD’s surveillance cameras. Instead, Wilson opted to postpone the installation of new SPD cameras in two new areas: the Capitol Hill nightlife district and an area around Garfield High School in the Central District. Wilson allowed new cameras to be installed in the Stadium District but only turned them on while Seattle was hosting World Cup matches this summer.
The NYU audit appears to have satisfied any qualms Wilson had about increasing the surveillance apparatus in Seattle.

“When I paused the expansion of CCTV, I did so because I believed we needed to ask some hard questions about data security and the protection of civil liberties, especially in the context of a federal administration that is targeting vulnerable communities and violating civil rights,” said Wilson. “After reviewing the evidence, the recommendations, and the safeguards available to us, I believe there is an important and responsible role for the RTCC within Seattle's public-safety system.”
The NYU Policing Project did not conduct any analysis around the cybersecurity risks of the data being collected by SPD.

Wilson said that Seattle has fewer surveillance cameras (so far) than many other American cities, an observation that hits differently at a time when the U.S. government is ramping up mass surveillance and the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is planning to deploy a domestic surveillance program in Seattle early next year.

Nevertheless, the surveillance cameras in the Stadium District will be turned back on immediately, and the City will proceed with the plans to procure and install cameras in the Capitol Hill nightlife district and the Central District.

“I also want to emphasize that these are not Flock cameras,” Wilson said. “Our system is managed by a company called Axon, and while there are obviously similarities in the technology, I think it's fair to say that Axon has a more responsive record.”

While less widely criticized than Flock, Axon has been receiving plenty of negative attention in its own right. In 2025 alone, Axon held $31.9 million in contracts with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). And just last week, a class action lawsuit was brought against Axon, alleging that Axon “blatantly violated” rules enacted by the California State Legislature regarding how Axon can capture, use, and store the data collected by their license plate readers.

“Like its competitors, Axon sells a centralized, vendor-controlled camera system that municipalities rent,” said Noah Williams, a local cybersecurity expert and member of advocacy group Communities Not Cameras. “Unlike Flock, it provides municipalities with a false sense of control over their camera footage.”

Wilson’s change of heart came in spite of the NYU audit clearly stating that SPD’s real-time crime center does involve real civil liberties risks. “Short of ceasing to retain RTCC data altogether, SPD cannot eliminate fully the risk that such data could be obtained and used for purposes prohibited under Washington law,” the report reads.
Vulnerabilities include data obtained via public disclosure laws, data obtained via subpoena of either the City or Axon, and data obtained illegally.

The City of Seattle paid the NYU Policing Project $223,000 for the audit, which found the same kind of sloppiness, lack of clear policies, and failure to live up to commitments in SPD’s surveillance program that were highlighted in the recent audits by the Seattle Office of the Auditor and the other from the Office of the Inspector General (OIG).

The original SPD surveillance pilot installed cameras in the Third Street corridor downtown, the Chinatown-International District (CID), and Aurora Avenue in North Seattle. Since that time, SPD has been given access to a large number of SDOT traffic safety cameras through their real-time crime center, as well as incorporating 23 private cameras from three private businesses, all of which are located in the Capitol Hill nightlife district where Wilson had said she was pausing SPD camera surveillance.
The private cameras in Capitol Hill were plugged into SPD’s real-time crime center with no notice to community members.

Ryan Talen, a nurse who lives in Capitol Hill and member of Communities Not Cameras, was unaware of the private cameras in his neighborhood being streamed into SPD’s real-time crime center until The Urbanist let him know after the press conference.
“It's a violation of our privacy,” Talen told The Urbanist .

The University of Pennsylvania is performing a separate audit in cooperation with the OIG, initiated during Mayor Bruce Harrell’s term, on the efficacy of SPD’s surveillance program. According to the NYU audit, the University of Pennsylvania’s audit won’t be completed until late next year.
Not everyone found the NYU audit as reassuring as Wilson.

“The report revealed what we've known since visiting the RTCC,” Communities Not Cameras said in a statement. “The recommendations to reform the RTCC in the report are half-measures. More oversight, audit policies and targeted use won't eliminate the fact that this system can and will be abused. Seattle has had a long history of police brutality and corruption and a short history of community healing. We need more of the latter. Addressing poverty, mental health and solving root causes of crime is what will make us safer.”

The NYU audit was conducted by a team of lawyers who found that there are “significant gaps” in the governance around the real-time crime center and made 19 recommendations that the authors say should be implemented if SPD continues their surveillance program.

The audit’s purpose was not to call out the general benefits and risks of SPD’s use of the real-time crime center, nor to make a recommendation on whether SPD’s surveillance should continue as designed.

However, in an apparent contradiction to Wilson’s claims that adding more surveillance cameras to SPD’s real-time crime center will make Seattle “safer,” the audit states, “Although the potential benefits of the RTCC as described by the City are plausible, the current research base supporting these benefits is thin. There is more robust research studying the public safety impacts of CCTVs on their own (i.e., not connected to an RTCC), but that research is best characterized as mixed.”

At the press conference, Wilson appeared to be focused more on the potential upsides of surveillance, albeit not currently backed by empirical studies, as opposed to the costs of expanding a technology that is known to aid in repression and authoritarian control.
“Once data exists, no city or agency can guarantee it will never be shared,” the audit emphasized.

According to the audit, there is an important distinction between targeted surveillance and what a real-time crime center does, which is categorized as “indiscriminate surveillance,” meaning the system surveils the public at large and collects information about people who are not suspected of any offense or wrongdoing. Indeed, due to the real-time crime center integrating many different technologies, the audit says, “The centralization of surveillance systems and data can enable far more powerful and intrusive forms of surveillance than any one system could accomplish on its own.”

When considering the many gaps, lack of clear policy, and lack of follow-through outlined in the audit, it’s striking that SPD had an entire two years since council approval of the real-time crime center surveillance pilot to make progress on these goals. The real-time crime center became operational on May 20, 2025 . Thus, the City has been operating this surveillance system for almost a year and a half without the development of basic policies for its use and the timely delivery of commitments SPD made as part of the City’s Surveillance Impact Review process. This lack of engaging seriously with the agreements and responsibilities around using such a robust surveillance apparatus seems in line with SPD’s past conduct regarding surveillance technologies in the City.

Auditors found that there is a lack of clarity around the approved purpose of SPD’s real-time crime center, centering on whether it should be used for low-level misdemeanors as well as more serious incidents. According to the report, SPD found guidance that limited surveillance use for misdemeanors “challenging from an operational perspective,” and yet the surveillance pilot was originally passed with the intention of reducing gun violence and human trafficking (despite no empirical evidence has proven that this kind of surveillance reduces either of these categories of crime).

In practice, the City is left with a surveillance system that could theoretically be used to police low-level issues like trespassing, public drug use, or shoplifting a package of diapers. Wilson refused to comment on this possibility other than to state that she’s looking forward to the University of Pennsylvania report that she expects to provide information as to how the real-time crime center is being used. Wilson’s answer suggests that the Mayor’s Office doesn’t expect to fully understand how SPD is using its surveillance system until two and a half years after it went operational.

While “real-time” is in the name, in practice the crime center is also used after the fact to investigate past events. If surveillance footage were to be used by SPD after the fact to track someone without a warrant, this usage would raise constitutional concerns and could potentially land the City in legal hot water. However, Wilson said SPD does not currently use the center for this purpose.

In addition, there are no firm policies in place for how to use the real-time crime center for large events. While passive monitoring of SPD camera feeds appears to be prohibited by policy, in practice, the auditors discovered that SPD created a case number for the entire World Cup and streamed live camera feeds through the real-time crime center throughout World Cup events.

Surveillance at protests is another gray area of SPD’s surveillance program, and the audit recommends SPD develop policies around the real-time crime center and protest activities that are protected by the First Amendment. Currently, demonstrations are captured by default if they take place where SPD and SDOT cameras are installed.

In order to improve transparency, the audit recommended that SPD fulfill its two outstanding Surveillance Impact Review commitments made in 2024: to have a public-facing dashboard that reports on real-time crime center use and to develop “an omnibus surveillance technology policy.” SPD told researchers that both projects were delayed but in process, and Wilson announced at the press conference that both projects would be completed. Why SPD would need an outside agency like the NYU Policing Project to recommend they fulfill their own previous commitments remains unclear.

“It's disappointing how unscientific this whole process is,” Ryan Talen, a nurse at Harborview and member of Communities Not Cameras, told The Urbanist . “It doesn't even feel like there are standards. You know, we're just accepting the SPD's word after they say they're going to do something, they're not doing it, and we're still moving forward with the program. What does that tell us about who's calling the shots around here? Clearly, not the people that elected Katie Wilson.”

The auditors also recommended SPD institute a five-day data retention policy, given that’s what SPD say they already do in practice, and that they institute a data retention policy around the data they clip and attach to investigations so they don’t retain the data indefinitely, long after a particular investigation is closed.

“Video clips and other data stored on Evidence.com are retained by SPD indefinitely, resulting in a substantial and growing repository of data that outside agencies could seek to obtain,” the report reads. Evidence.com is Axon’s cloud-based evidence management system.

Another recommendation suggests that SPD should publish “in a clear and conspicuous location on its website” a full list of the tools and features it is using — and seeking approval to use — in its real-time crime center at least twice a year, as well as institute a policy for regular internal audits of the real-time crime center. In addition to internal audits, NYU researchers suggested the OIG should add identifying material changes to SPD’s use of surveillance tools to its annual audit requirements.

What the audit fails to address is what to do if SPD fails to implement these recommendations in practice. The OIG audit from October, for example, showed that SPD has already failed in its commitment to make sure every camera has privacy masking in place if it’s facing a private residence. And SPD has failed to live up to commitments it made in the Surveillance Impact Review back in 2024, even though two years have passed.

articles.title: Latest Look at 'Tactical Urbanism' Planned for Stadium District
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A street transformation is coming to the Stadium District's front porch, with plans advancing for " tactical urbanism " along Occidental Avenue South near Lumen Field and T-Mobile Park. The quick-build changes tabbed for mid-2027 are intended to test a longer-term vision for a corridor that gets heavy usage on event days and is often trying to serve multiple different types of street users.
The Occidental Promenade is set to be the most visible product of Seattle's new People Streets and Public Spaces program, funded by the 2024 Seattle Transportation Levy .

Former Mayor Bruce Harrell directly inserted the promenade into his levy proposal, with support of stadium boosters including Seahawks chief operating officer David Young. The idea grew out of earlier efforts to improve Occidental Avenue, including a stadium district study that developed a streetscape plan in 2015, concepts that were ultimately put on a shelf to collect dust.

Final plans for the "near term" upgrades presented last week to Pioneer Square's Preservation District Board for approval show include chicanes, planters, street seating and micromobility corrals intended to carve out space along the wide street for pedestrian use. With the chicanes in place, the hope is for calmer traffic as drivers are prevented from picking up speed along a straight route of travel.

In a departure from most standard transportation projects, the Occidental Promenade is being managed by the Seattle Parks Foundation, in coordination with the Pioneer Square Alliance. The Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) will handle the design work. The Parks Foundation, a private non-profit organization that often bridges the gap between the City of Seattle and neighborhood groups interested in improving their park spaces, describes the promenade project as enabling a more "vibrant stadium district, providing street amenities and flexibility for the various users and venues."
The foundation also outlines a goal of better managing vending along the street. A future vending pilot program is expected to come back for separate approval at a later date.

"I would suggest it's probably the most hardworking street in downtown. We've got freight loading and unloading for the stadiums, which can range from, on a Taylor Swift concert, upwards of 20 to 25 semi trailers," said Jessa Timmer, Deputy Director at the Alliance for Pioneer Square, told the preservation board. "We've got pedestrian folks – during World Cup, we had, I don't even know how many, 150,000 to 200,000 pedestrians coming through Pioneer Square and this corridor. We've got back of house for many restaurants and businesses, sometimes front of house for those businesses."
"It's really a wide-ranging kind of ecosystem that's back here," Timmer said.

The improvements planned largely reinforce that ecosystem. The back-angle parking found across the street from Lumen Field will be retained, with a delineated walking path connecting the new nodes of pedestrian activity. Those paths will be most likely to be used on event days, creating a more orderly dispersal of pedestrian traffic when crowds are at their biggest.
It's less clear how utilized the planned seating will be on non-game days, with the street furniture essentially existing as an island in the middle of the street in some places.

"Our approach is really looking at a surface treatment and edge delineation to calm traffic and really work to improve that legibility and increase space for non-vehicular uses," SDOT project manager Ian Macek said.

The timeline to make the changes is currently dependent on Seattle City Light, which is planning work along Occidental in 2027, with promenade work to follow. But this phase will essentially act as a pilot to see how carving out pedestrian spaces works when it comes to the day-to-day operation of the street.

Though SDOT does need to receive a Certificate of Approval from the Pioneer Square Preservation Board to move forward with construction, that might not necessarily be the case with similar projects in the future. A legislative change put forward by Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck would explicitly exempt traffic control devices from requirements for buy-in from historic district boards like Pioneer Square's. Though the change has received a fair amount of pushback from historic preservation advocates , it is still heading for a council vote by early next year.

"These these improvements are inspired by the neighborhood context," Macek said. "They are temporary and reversible, and so this is really seen as a way to help pilot some of these options to see how they work, and also help inform that longer term before we commit to a design and advance that forward to be able to test things out, and really looking at materials that aren't impacting the historic resources along the corridor."
While billed as a "quick-build" intervention, the Occidental Promenade will still take more than two years from the launch of planning in early 2025 to implementation in mid-2027.

Other People Streets and Public Spaces projects are also moving forward at SDOT, including pedestrian plazas planned in Upper Queen Anne, Admiral, and Delridge. Unlike Occidental, those projects weren't specifically named in the 2024 levy but grew out of neighborhood support for creating pedestrian-forward spaces, building on past programs like the Pavement to Parks program abandoned under former Mayor Jenny Durkan.

Final approval to move forward with the Occidental Promenade is expected at a Pioneer Square Preservation District Board meeting before the end of the year. You can review the full plan set for Occidental Avenue here . The department also has active surveys up on SW Lander Street , 18th Avenue SW , and W Crocket Street .
